# Scoping canvas

A one-page, multi-section definition of what an initiative actually covers — problem, goal, in scope, out of scope, team, timeline, assumptions — before anyone starts work on it.

Family: Problem definition · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

A scoping canvas is a one-page definition of what an initiative actually covers, built before anyone starts work on it — not a project plan, and not a full charter, just the boundary-setting document that keeps a team from discovering three weeks in that they disagreed about what was in scope. Unlike most tools in this catalogue, a canvas is genuinely defined by which sections apply to the situation, the same way a real Business Model Canvas or lean scoping exercise is — problem/goal/in-scope/out-of-scope/team/timeline/assumptions is the default set, not a rigid universal structure.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- An initiative is real enough to commit time to, but its boundaries haven't been written down anywhere a disagreement could be checked against.
- Multiple people or teams are involved, and 'what's actually in scope' has already come up as a question once.
- You want a fast way to see what's still undefined — a thin section here is a real gap, not just an editing task.

Not when:

- The initiative is small enough that one person can hold the whole scope in their head with no real risk of drift — a canvas adds ceremony without adding value there.
- You need a full charter with a resourced budget and formal sign-off — a kaizen event charter or business case is the right tool for that weight of commitment.
- The boundaries are already written down and agreed somewhere else — don't duplicate an existing source of truth.

## How to fill it in

- **problem** — What's the situation, and why does it matter now? One or two sentences, not a full background essay.
- **goal** — What does this initiative need to achieve, specifically enough that you'd know if it succeeded?
- **in-scope** — What's genuinely in scope — drafted from your notes, then yours to correct.
- **out-of-scope** — What's deliberately excluded, and why — an empty out-of-scope section is itself a finding, not just unfilled.
- **team** — Who's involved, and in what role?
- **timeline** — What are the key milestones or phases?
- **assumptions** — What has to be true for this to work, or what's constraining it?

## What good looks like

The example below scopes a kaizen event that picks up directly where a prior A3's countermeasures left off — tightly bounded to one line, one procedure, explicitly deferring the adjacent line and any capital spend rather than letting scope creep in by default.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/scoping-canvas

## Common mistakes

- **Leaving out-of-scope empty because nothing's been explicitly excluded yet.** — An empty out-of-scope section almost never means nothing's excluded — it usually means the boundary hasn't been thought through yet, which is exactly the ambiguity this canvas exists to catch before it causes a real disagreement.
- **Writing a goal statement vague enough that almost any outcome would count as success.** — A goal that can't fail isn't a real goal — the same discipline an A3's problem statement or a business case's cost-of-inaction section already holds itself to.
- **Treating the canvas as a one-time exercise nobody revisits once the initiative starts.** — Scope drifts in real work — a canvas that's never checked against again is ceremony, not a working document.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **A3 problem solving** — A recurring problem an A3 surfaces sometimes needs work bigger than one countermeasure can carry — that's exactly when it graduates into a scoped initiative of its own.

Downstream:

- **Kaizen event charter** — Once an initiative is scoped and worth a dedicated event, the charter is where it gets resourced, dated, and given a roster — heavier commitment than a canvas alone implies.
- **Business case** — An initiative whose value needs to be argued for, not just scoped, is where a business case's investment/value-driver discipline takes over.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding where the real boundary between in-scope and out-of-scope actually sits
- Deciding whether a goal statement is specific enough to know later whether it was hit

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting each section's bullets from a rough description of the initiative
- Flagging a section that's too thin to mean anything yet, rather than padding it

Drudgery — automated:

- Formatting the canvas and keeping every section on one page
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
